clue.text: "Hamleigh's servant sitting behind, walled in by a portmanteau and a ——" (M. E. Braddon, Mount Royal)

definitions.text: "Hamleigh's servant sitting behind, walled in by a portmanteau and a ——" (M. E. Braddon, Mount Royal)

parts.words: "Hamleigh's servant sitting behind, walled in by a portmanteau and a ——" (M. E. Braddon, Mount Royal)
parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank quotation: the missing words name a hinged leather travelling case that sits beside the portmanteau

explanation.surface: A servant perches at the back of a carriage, boxed in by luggage, in a line from a Victorian novel.
explanation.walkthrough: Mary Elizabeth Braddon's novel Mount Royal supplies the line; the gap is a piece of luggage named after a Victorian prime minister.
explanation.definitionFit: The quotation lists luggage, and this hinged leather travelling case is the item that completes the list.

clue.text: An eye for Neville Smith's eponymous character?

definitions.meaning: a private eye, a detective in slang
Neville Smith wrote the 1971 film whose title names its would-be detective hero

explanation.definitionFit: Slang for a private detective, and the title role of Neville Smith's film about a Liverpool bingo caller playing sleuth.

clue.text: New presentation of Tosca in Berkshire …

definitions.note: the definition names a place found in Berkshire, a town rather than the county itself

indicators.note: a new presentation of an opera restages it, and here the letters of its title are restaged in a fresh order

explanation.surface: A fresh production of Puccini's opera is being staged somewhere in Berkshire.
explanation.walkthrough: 'New presentation of' rearranges TOSCA. Ascot is a Berkshire town famous for its racecourse; the ellipsis carries the reading on into the next clue.
explanation.definitionFit: The town with the royal racecourse lies in the English county of Berkshire, west of London.

clue.text: … trial acts rewritten for composer

indicators.note: a text that is rewritten is put together again differently, so the letters are reordered

explanation.surface: The acts of an opera about a court case are revised by its musician.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rewritten' rearranges TRIAL ACTS.
explanation.definitionFit: Domenico Scarlatti was an Italian baroque keyboard composer, and his father Alessandro wrote operas.

clue.text: Take nothing from egg-shaped poet His turned the live air sick" (Tennyson)

indicators.note: to take something from a word is to remove it, so the zero is lifted out of the synonym

parts.note: egg-shaped means ovoid
nothing is zero, the letter O

explanation.surface: Remove the zero from an oval-shaped poet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Take ... from' removes one O from OVOID. The held clue has the following clue's Tennyson quotation run on after 'poet'; those words play no part.
explanation.definitionFit: Publius Ovidius Naso, author of the Metamorphoses, was a Roman poet.

clue.text: "His -turned the live air sick " (Tennyson)

parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank quotation from Tennyson's Maud, where the missing word is the scents given off by the rose

explanation.surface: A line from Tennyson about a fragrance that sours the very air.
explanation.walkthrough: The line comes from Maud: the speaker complains that the rose's scents turned the living air sick.
explanation.definitionFit: Essences are concentrated scents or perfumes, which fits a flower whose smell poisons the air.

clue.text: George Russell's Irish version of Norse gods

parts.note: AE was the pen name of the Irish poet George Russell; with the possessive it gives AE'S

explanation.surface: An Irish poet retells the Scandinavian myths in his own version.
explanation.walkthrough: George Russell signed his work AE; the possessive supplies the S. 'version of' links the pieces to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The Aesir are the principal family of deities in Norse mythology, including Odin and Thor.

clue.text: New hedonism for American adaptor of Romeo and Juliet

definitions.text: American adaptor of Romeo and Juliet

indicators.note: a new version of something is a remade one, so the letters of the next word are made into a different order

explanation.surface: A fresh hedonism inspires the American who reworked Shakespeare's tragedy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'New' rearranges HEDONISM.
explanation.definitionFit: Stephen Sondheim wrote the lyrics for West Side Story, the musical that transplants Shakespeare's lovers to New York.

clue.text: Hichens's was banged up

parts.note: Robert Hichens wrote the 1908 novel A ... in Prison, so his title figure was locked away

explanation.surface: Something belonging to the novelist Hichens got locked up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Banged up' is British slang for imprisoned; Robert Hichens's novel is A Spirit in Prison.
explanation.definitionFit: The title of Hichens's novel places a soul or ghost behind bars, so the thing jailed is that ghostly being.

clue.text: Working of plot perhaps from mischance?

indicators.note: the answer is made from the letters of the following word, reworked into a new order

explanation.surface: Could a story's plot come about through an unlucky accident?
explanation.walkthrough: Rearrange MISCHANCE; 'from' signals that the answer is made out of its letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The mechanics of something are its workings, as when one discusses how a story's plot is engineered.

clue.text: Kent warship

parts.note: Alexander Kent wrote naval novels about Richard Bolitho, one titled ... of War

explanation.definitionFit: A single-masted sailing vessel, and the small warship of Alexander Kent's Bolitho novel title.

clue.text: Accommodation suggested by Bowen and Hailey

definitions.text: Accommodation suggested by Bowen and Hailey

parts.words: Accommodation suggested by Bowen and Hailey
parts.note: Elizabeth Bowen's first novel and Arthur Hailey's 1965 bestseller are both titled after a place where travellers pay for rooms

explanation.surface: Two novelists, Bowen and Hailey, each point to somewhere to stay.
explanation.walkthrough: Elizabeth Bowen's first novel (1927) and Arthur Hailey's bestseller (1965) share a one-word title naming such a building, so together they suggest the plural.
explanation.definitionFit: Establishments offering paid rooms to travellers are the accommodation both book titles name.

clue.text: Faulkner's was in the dust

parts.note: William Faulkner's 1948 novel is titled ... in the Dust, so his figure was in the dust

explanation.surface: Something of Faulkner's lay in the dirt.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue completes the title of Faulkner's novel Intruder in the Dust.
explanation.definitionFit: Faulkner's title names an unwelcome trespasser, the figure who was in the dust.

clue.text: Steven upset by happenings in a book?

indicators.note: something upset is knocked over and disordered, so the letters of the name are scrambled

explanation.surface: Steven is distressed by things that happen in a novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' rearranges STEVEN; the question mark admits that the definition fits any incidents, not only those in books.
explanation.definitionFit: Events are occurrences, the incidents that make up a plot.

clue.text: For example the French love of Shakespearian knight

parts.note: l' is the French word for the before a vowel
amour is French for love

explanation.surface: Take, say, the French romance of one of Shakespeare's chivalrous knights.
explanation.walkthrough: L' is the elided form of the French article le or la, used before a vowel as in l'amour.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Eglamour is the knight who helps Silvia escape in The Two Gentlemen of Verona.

clue.text: A shoo-in from Francis

definitions.meaning: a sure winner, something certain to succeed
Dick Francis's first racing thriller, 1962, carries this title

explanation.definitionFit: Racing slang for a horse certain to win, and the title of Dick Francis's debut novel.

clue.text: Hillerman's participants inanimate here

parts.note: Tony Hillerman's novel is ... of the Dead, a venue where the dancers are lifeless

explanation.surface: In a Hillerman story, the people taking part here are lifeless.
explanation.walkthrough: Tony Hillerman's Navajo mystery is Dance Hall of the Dead (1973); 'participants inanimate' are the dead who dance there.
explanation.definitionFit: A dance hall is a public room for dancing, and Hillerman's title fills it with the dead.

clue.text: Paper going to Touchstone's head?

definitions.meaning: a large size of writing or printing paper
Touchstone is the jester in As You Like It, so his headgear would be a jester's cap

explanation.definitionFit: A traditional large sheet size of paper, and the jester's cap that Shakespeare's clown Touchstone would wear.

clue.text: He gave us a start in life and told us it goes on

definitions.text: He gave us a start in life and told us it goes on

parts.words: He gave us a start in life and told us it goes on
parts.note: Alan ... wrote the novel A Start in Life and its sequel Life Goes On

explanation.surface: A mentor launched us in our careers and assured us that things continue.
explanation.walkthrough: Alan Sillitoe's picaresque novel A Start in Life (1970) was followed by Life Goes On (1985).
explanation.definitionFit: The Nottingham novelist Alan Sillitoe wrote both titles the clue paraphrases.

clue.text: Provenance of Puzo protagonist

parts.note: Mario Puzo's Godfather, Vito Corleone, was born in the town of Corleone on a Mediterranean island

explanation.surface: Where Mario Puzo's hero came from.
explanation.walkthrough: Vito Corleone of The Godfather takes his name from Corleone, his birthplace.
explanation.definitionFit: The Mediterranean island off the toe of Italy is the birthplace of Puzo's Don Corleone.

clue.text: Sententious like garden feature?

definitions.meaning: given to pithy maxims and aphorisms
a garden gnome is an ornamental feature, so gnome-like describes it

explanation.definitionFit: Gnomic means aphoristic, full of maxims, and read whimsically it means resembling a garden gnome.

clue.text: Poet sharing work in hand with Graves is able to include more changes

definitions.text: Poet sharing work in hand with Graves

indicators.note: to include something is to hold it within, so the reworked letters go inside

parts.note: is able means can

indicators.note: changes says the letters of the preceding word are altered into another order

explanation.surface: A poet who collaborated with Graves is capable of fitting in further revisions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'changes' rearranges the clue's 'more', and 'to include' places the result inside the synonym for 'is able'. Norman Cameron was Robert Graves's friend and collaborator in Majorca.
explanation.definitionFit: Norman Cameron, Scottish poet, worked closely with Robert Graves and Laura Riding in Majorca.

clue.text: Signal at temporary stopover for poets David, Joseph and Roy

parts.note: a camp is a temporary place to stop and stay
a bell rings as a signal

explanation.surface: A signal sounds at a temporary halt for several poets.
explanation.walkthrough: The pieces go in the order of the answer, the stopover before the signal. David, Joseph and Roy Campbell were all poets.
explanation.definitionFit: The surname is shared by poets David Campbell (Australian), Joseph Campbell (Irish) and Roy Campbell (South African).

clue.text: Misleading encouragement for woman in Leonard title

definitions.text: Misleading encouragement for woman in Leonard title

parts.words: Misleading encouragement for woman in Leonard title
parts.note: Elmore Leonard's novel La... names a Miami district, not a cheer, though the word is what an audience shouts to a female performer

explanation.surface: A deceptive cheer for a woman appears in a Leonard title.
explanation.walkthrough: Elmore Leonard's LaBrava (1983) takes its name from a character, so the cheer for a female performer within it is misleading.
explanation.definitionFit: The feminine form of bravo is shouted to applaud a woman singer, and it ends Leonard's title LaBrava.

clue.text: Bulwer-Lytton's gentleman in chapel, hampered by scepticism

indicators.note: the letters sit in the run of the words that follow

explanation.surface: Bulwer-Lytton's gentleman sits in a chapel, troubled by religious doubt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' places the answer across 'chaPEL HAMpered'; 'by scepticism' only finishes the picture.
explanation.definitionFit: Bulwer-Lytton's novel Pelham, or the Adventures of a Gentleman (1828) is named for its dandy hero.

clue.text: It does not matter much what a man provided he —— something" (Samuel Butler, Note-books)

definitions.text: It does not matter much what a man provided he —— something" (Samuel Butler, Note-books)

parts.words: It does not matter much what a man provided he —— something" (Samuel Butler, Note-books)
parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank quotation; Butler's full line is that it hardly matters what a man loathes, so long as he loathes something

explanation.surface: Samuel Butler muses that a man's dislikes matter less than having some.
explanation.walkthrough: The full aphorism reads: 'It does not matter much what a man hates, provided he hates something.' The held clue has dropped the first verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Butler's line turns on detesting something, and the verb to fill the gap means detests.

clue.text: Light as Porter's horse and rider

definitions.meaning: light in colour, faint or wan
Katherine Anne Porter's novella is ... Horse, ... Rider, the same adjective applied to both

explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means light or faint in colour, and it describes both horse and rider in Katherine Anne Porter's title.

clue.text: Caspary's 27, a student with an emanation

parts.note: L is a learner, the letter on a British learner driver's plate
an aura is a subtle emanation surrounding a person or thing

explanation.surface: A character in a Caspary novel is a student with a strange glow about her.
explanation.walkthrough: 27 points to the answer at 27 across, CHARACTER: Vera Caspary's novel Laura names its heroine. The 'a' and 'with' only link the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Vera Caspary's 1943 mystery is named for its heroine, the woman the detective falls for.

clue.text: Smiles raised, this book showing personality

definitions.meaning: Samuel Smiles, author of Self-Help, also published a book of this title in 1871

explanation.definitionFit: Samuel Smiles's improving 1871 book shares its title with the word for a person's moral nature or personality.

clue.text: No peril shall upset creator of indiscernible Iantalus by

indicators.note: something upset is overturned and thrown into disorder, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: No danger shall disturb the author of a hard-to-see figure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' rearranges NO PERIL SHALL. Ralph Ellison wrote Invisible Man; the held definition is an OCR garble, plainly meaning the author of the indiscernible man.
explanation.definitionFit: Ralph Ellison's 1952 novel Invisible Man tells of a Black narrator society refuses to see.
